Learning Objectives
Identify the mechanical and material properties of orthopaedic materials.
Examine the various biologic reactions to orthopaedic biomaterials and their potential
corrosion and degradation.
Assess biomaterials and determine if they are made from organic or inorganic components
and how they are intended to interact with biologic systems.
Assess biocompatibility and minimize detrimental local or systemic responses, resisting
mechanical, chemical, and biologic degradation.
Review the current definition of and implement appropriate strategies for select appropriate
orthopaedic materials.

Most orthopaedic implants are used in load-bearing applications, to replace damaged or
diseased tissue (eg, joint replacement), or to provide structural support during healing (eg,
internal fixation).
They must have structural properties appropriate for their intended applications.
They must be sufficiently strong and have sufficient fatigue resistance to withstand any applied
loads, and it is important that their stiffness is tuned to positively influence healing.
Mechanical properties are the physical properties that a material exhibits upon the application
of force.
Stress is the force applied over a unit of area of a material. The Standard International (SI)
unit for stress is newton/meter2 (N/m2) or Pascals (Pa).
A force that acts perpendicularly to a surface results in a normal stress.
A force that acts tangentially to a surface results in a shear stress.
A stress is tensile if it stretches the material on which it acts.
A stress is compressive if it squeezes the material on which it acts.
A stress is torsional if it rotates the material on which it acts.
Strain is the deformation of a material by a force acting on a material or the change in the
length of a material under stress compared to the original length of the material relieved of
stress. Consequently, strain is unitless and generally is reported as a percentage (%) or unit
length of change per unit length of an object. The types of strain associated with normal and
shear stress are called normal strain and shear strain, respectively. Like stress, strain may be
either tensile or compressive.
Material strength is the load-carrying capacity of a material. A plot of the deformation of a
material versus the stress acting on the material or object is called the stress-strain curve
(Figure 1). This can be used to describe the strength of a material independently of its cross-
sectional area. Material properties generally reported are using the term strength rather
than stress.

Figure 1 Graph shows the various components and relationships in the stress-strain curve.
Note that the slope of elastic recovery is the same as the Young modulus. (Reproduced from
Ayers RA, Singh K: Biomaterials, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review,
ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 607-619.)
Toughness is the area under the stress-strain curve. It describes the energy needed to cause
the material to fail (Figure 2).
Figure 2 Graph shows that toughness is the energy absorbed prior to failure, indicated by
the area under the stress-strain curve. These two materials are equally tough (the areas
under the curve are the same), even though one is stiff and brittle and the other is flexible
and ductile. (Reproduced from Buckwalter JA, Einhorn TA, Simon SR, eds: Biomechanics, in

Orthopaedic Basic Science: Biology and Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System, ed 2.
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2000.)
The modulus of elasticity (also known as the Young modulus) is a unique property of a
material defined by the slope of the linear portion of the stress-strain curve (Figure 1). The
modulus of elasticity is a measure of the atomic bonds in a material that resist deformation
and return the material to its original shape. The modulus of elasticity does not correlate
with the strength of a material (Table 1). A high modulus of elasticity indicates that a material
is stiffer and more resistant to elastic deformation than a material with a lower modulus of
elasticity.

anatomic location and orientation.
Reproduced from Ayers RA, Singh K: Biomaterials, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive
Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020,
pp 607-619.
As the stress on a material increases relative to the deformation of the material, the slope of
the stress-strain curve changes at the yield point (Figure 1). Up to the yield point, the
material is operating elastically, which means that if the stress is removed, the strain on the
material will decrease as the material returns to its original shape. The yield point is the
transition between elastic and plastic deformation. If the stress on a material reaches the
yield point, the material begins to demonstrate plastic behavior and is permanently
deformed. Beyond the yield point, the stress on a material only increases slightly; however,
the material undergoes considerable deformation as the result of plastic deformation.
The maximum stress that a material or object can support before failure is its yield point.
Beyond this point of maximal stress, stress decreases as the material fails.
A material can be classified as brittle or ductile based on its stress-strain curve (Figure 3).
A brittle material exhibits very little plastic deformation before failure. Examples of brittle
materials are ceramics such as alumina, hydroxyapatite, titanium, concrete, cast iron, silica,
and thermoset polymers such as Bakelite.
A ductile material exhibits large amounts of plastic deformation before failure. Stainless
steel, cobalt-chromium (CoCr) alloys, titanium alloys, copper, magnesium, nylon, and Teflon
are examples of ductile materials (Figure 3).

Figure 3 Graph shows the various stress-strain relationships. High strength with low ductility
is indicative of a ceramic. High strength with high ductility is typical of steels, certain
polymers, and viscoelastic responses of materials. Low strength with high ductility is typical
of most polymers, such as rubber, silicone, elastin, and collagen. (Reproduced from Ayers RA,
Singh K: Biomaterials, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3.
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 607-619.)
Isotropic materials (eg, stainless steel, titanium alloys) have the same mechanical properties
along all axes or in all directions within the material.
Anisotropic materials (eg, bone, cartilage, muscle, ligament, carbon-fiber composites) exhibit
varying mechanical properties along each axis or in different directions within the material
under loading (Figure 4). This anisotropic behavior is a result of specifically oriented
constituent parts of these materials (eg, fibrils or crystals).

Figure 4 Graph shows that cortical bone tissue is anisotropic. Specimens taken via different
orientations from the cortex of a long bone and loaded in tension will exhibit different stress-
strain behavior. In general, the longitudinal direction exhibits a higher elastic modulus and
greater strength, whereas the transverse direction exhibits the lowest elastic modulus and
strength. (Adapted with permission from Nordin M, Frankel VH, eds: Basic Biomechanics of the
Musculoskeletal System, ed 2. Philadelphia, PA, Lea & Febiger, 1989.)
All materials except for very brittle materials can be considered viscoelastic, exhibiting
viscosity in that they resist shear and strain if subjected to stress and exhibiting elasticity in
that they undergo distortion if subjected to stress and return rapidly to their original state
after the stress is removed (Figure 5). Viscoelastic properties are time- or rate-dependent.

Figure 5 Graph shows that cortical bone tissue is viscoelastic. Specimens of cortical bone
loaded at three different rates will exhibit three different stress-strain curves, with elastic
modulus and strength increasing as the rate increases. (Reproduced with permission from
Burstein AH, Wright TM, eds: Fundamentals of Orthopaedic Biomechanics. Baltimore, MD,
Williams & Wilkins, 1994.)
Hysteresis is the dependence of the stress-strain curve on its present and past environments
because the material may be in more than one internal state. Hysteresis is represented by the
area between the loaded and unloaded regions of a stress-strain curve (Figure 6).

Figure 6 Graph shows that if a specimen of cortical bone is loaded to point A, and the load is
released, the bone immediately returns to its original length; however, not along the same
path as the loading process. If a specimen of cortical bone is loaded to point B, and the load is
released, elongation does not immediately return to zero. Several seconds are required before
the specimen returns to zero. If a specimen of cortical bone is loading to point C, and the load
is released, change in length results that is not reversible. (Reproduced with permission from
Burstein AH, Wright TM, eds: Fundamentals of Orthopaedic Biomechanics. Baltimore, MD,
Williams & Wilkins, 1994.)
Creep is the increased deformation of a material over time in response to the application of a
constant force (Figure 7). An example of creep occurs in a rubber band wrapped around a
book for an extended period.

Figure 7 Graphs show typical compressive creep and recovery (A) and ramp loading and stress
relaxation behaviors (B) of hydrated, soft, collagenous tissues, such as articular cartilage,
intervertebral disk, and meniscus. (Reproduced from Buckwalter JA, Einhorn TA, Simon SR, eds:
Biomechanics, in Orthopaedic Basic Science: Biology and Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal
System, ed 2. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2000.)
Stress relaxation is a decrease in the stress on a material over time as the result of a constant
displacement within the material or object.
Fatigue failure is failure related to the cyclic loading of a material (Figure 8). This is the most
common mode of failure in orthopaedic applications. If a material is subjected to a dynamic
load with a large number of loading cycles, failure will occur at loads below the yield point of
the material. The strength of a material decreases with an increasing number of loading cycles.
Fatigue failure consists of three steps: the initiation of a crack, propagation of the crack, and
catastrophic failure.
The endurance limit or fatigue strength is a characteristic only of ferrous alloys, such as
stainless steel. Nonferrous alloys, such as aluminum or titanium alloys, ceramics, and
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:26 PM
AAOS | Orthopaedic Biomaterials
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002108
10/44

polymers, do not exhibit endurance limits. The endurance limit is defined as the strength of a
ferrous alloy after 106 loading cycles.
The polar moment of inertia is a quantity determined by the cross-sectional area and
distribution of an object around a neutral axis upon torsional loading of the object. The greater
the polar moment of inertia, the stiffer and stronger the object. The SI unit is m4. A thicker or
larger part of a device is more resistant to increased loads and deformations than a similar
thinner or smaller part. For example, a spine surgeon may select a 6.5-mm spine rod over a
5.5-mm spine rod to create a stiffer construct and more rigidly fix the spine.
Figure 8 Schematic shows the fatigue test. Carefully machined specimens are cyclically loaded to
different levels of maximum stress (σ = F/A0) and the number of cycles to failure (N) is recorded.
Specimens fail quickly if cyclic stress is high and after more cycles if cyclic stress is low. For many
materials, a lower limit of cyclic stress will result in fatigue failure. This lower limit is called the
endurance limit (EL), or fatigue limit. Ts = tensile strength, Ys = yield strength. (Reproduced from
Jenkins DR, Moore DC: Biomaterials in orthopaedic practice, in Aaron RK, ed: Orthopaedic Basic
Science: Foundations of Clinical Practice, ed 5. Rosemont, IL American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2021, pp 63-75.)
Properties of Biomaterials

A biomaterial is a synthetic material derived from organic or inorganic components and
intended to interact with biologic systems, replacing or supporting the form and/or function of
native tissues. The material properties of a biomaterial are dictated:
By its structure (eg, elemental composition, atomic bonding, atomic organization, or
crystallinity);
By its processing (eg, any one of hundreds of manufacturing techniques, including but not
limited to casting, forging, extrusion, injection molding, sintering, welding, solid-state
bonding, or filament winding) (Figure 9); and
By its biocompatibility (eg, interactions between a biomaterial and the host biologic system
will lead to success or failure of the material).
Figure 9 Illustration shows that the relationship between properties and performance is related
to microscopic structure, chemical constituents, and how the material is synthesized (processed).
(Reproduced from Gibon E, Goodman SB: The biologic response to bearing materials, in Mont
MA, Tanzer M, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Hip and Knee, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017, pp 367-375.)
Biocompatibility

Biocompatibility is defined as an acceptable host response for a specific application of a
natural or synthetic biomaterial. It is neither an intrinsic property nor a state of a material, but
rather a series of responses that allow the material to fulfill its intended function.
Inert: elicits little or no host response
Interactive: elicits a beneficial response from the host, like bony ingrowth and porous
tantalum
Viable: implanted biomaterials that incorporate and attract cells and are then absorbed
and/or remodeled by the host (eg, biodegradable ceramic or polymeric scaffolds for
functional tissue engineering)
Allogeneic: tissues obtained from a donor or cultured in vitro prior to host implantation
Autogeneic: tissue or organ transplanted into a new position within or on the same individual
Incompatible: elicits a destructive immunologic or inflammatory response (eg, organ
rejection).
Metals
Metals typically are hard, durable, and strong materials.
Metals can be a single element (eg, titanium) or multiple metallic and nonmetallic elements,
called a metal alloy (eg, stainless steel—iron, chromium, nickel, molybdenum, and carbon).
Several alloys are commonly used in orthopaedics (Table 2):
Stainless steel
Cobalt alloys
Titanium and titanium alloys

Metal alloys are excellent orthopaedic biomaterials because of their fatigue resistance
and ductility. Metals are crystalline arrays. Within each crystal, the atoms of the metal
are regularly spaced and packed in specific configurations, allowing the atoms to share
their outer valence electrons (metallic bonding), which are responsible for their excellent
ductility, heat, and electrical conductivity. Alloys are solutions of different metals or of
metals and nonmetallic elements. Metals typically are fabricated by casting, forging, or
extrusion (Figure 10).

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002108

Figure 10 Schematic diagram shows stages in the processing of metal alloys into
orthopaedic implants. (Adapted with permission from Ratner BD, Hoffman AS, Schoen FJ,
Lemons JE, eds: Biomaterials Science: An Introduction to Materials in Medicine, ed 2. San
Diego, CA, Academic Press, 2004, p 138.)
In casting, molten metal is poured into a mold. Objects or parts formed in this way tend
to be weaker and require further processing to gain strength. In forging, hot mechanical
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:26 PM
AAOS | Orthopaedic Biomaterials
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002108
16/44

forming of metal using hammers, presses, or forging machines is used to form a metal
object or part by compressing, bending, or otherwise shaping a mass of heated,
malleable metal. Forged metal objects tend to be stronger than cast metal objects. In
extrusion, metal is heated and forced through a die to obtain a continuous object with a
specifically shaped cross-section, such as a duct or tube.
Stainless Steel
The most commonly used stainless steel alloy is A316L, in which iron is alloyed with substantial
amounts of chromium to enhance corrosion resistance and nickel to enhance its corrosion
resistance and formability.

Stainless Steel
Because they contain potentially allergenic metals, notably nickel, chromium, and
molybdenum, A316L and other steels may induce an allergic response. The ductility of
stainless steel is important in applications such as bone screws, in which a definite yield
point of bone allows the surgeon to feel the beginning of plastic deformation. Because
steel has a single yield point at which the metal begins to deform, the surgeon can feel if
the bone begins to yield before the screw yielding, unlike titanium, which has a range of
yield points. Carbon is added to impart strength to steel; however, it must remain in
solution with molten iron to do so. If the carbon concentration of the molten iron-carbon
mixture is too high, iron carbides (Fe3C) segregate, forming a brittle ceramic phase and
substantially weakening the resulting steel by making it prone to corrosion-related
fracture. Stainless steel is susceptible to pitting and crevice corrosion, although its
corrosion resistance can be improved by increased nitrogen alloying.
Cobalt Alloys
Cobalt alloys are among the strongest orthopaedic implant materials and are suitable for high-
load applications that require longevity.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:26 PM
AAOS | Orthopaedic Biomaterials
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002108
17/44


Cobalt Alloys
They consist of approximately 70% cobalt and 27% chromium by atomic content, with
small percentages of molybdenum and carbon included to enhance strength and
ductility. The predominant fabrication technique for cobalt alloys is casting.
Titanium and Titanium Alloys
Pure titanium typically is used for fracture fixation at anatomic sites at which large loads are
not expected (eg, maxilla, wrist, phalanges).

Titanium and Titanium Alloys
Pure titanium is less ductile than stainless steel and is highly susceptible to notch
hardening and stress corrosion cracking, explaining the screw and rod breakage often
noted with titanium implants. For higher-strength applications, titanium alloys must be
used (eg, Ti-6Al-4V, which consists of titanium with atomic contents of 6% aluminum for
increased strength and 4% vanadium for increased ductility).
Tantalum
Tantalum is a transitional metal that is highly corrosion-resistant. Tantalum facilitates bone
ingrowth into a prosthetic device.
Zirconium
Zirconium is a biocompatible metallic element in the same family as titanium.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:26 PM
AAOS | Orthopaedic Biomaterials
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002108
18/44


Zirconium
It is a hard, malleable, and ductile metal that is highly resistant to corrosion. The surface
layer is oxidized (to form zirconium dioxide [ZrO2]) to increase wear resistance
(proprietary technology).
Ceramics
Ceramics are strong, brittle, and corrosion-resistant materials.
They are made of elements linked to one another by covalent or ionic bonds, and many are
oxides of metallic elements, such as alumina (Al2O3) and zirconia (ZrO2), or oxides of silicon
(such as SiO2) or of silicon in combination with metallic or other elements.
Ceramic materials are stiff and brittle but very strong under compressive loads and have
gained favor in two types of orthopaedic applications:
As bearings (eg, ceramic-on-polyethylene and ceramic-on-ceramic) in total joint
arthroplasty because ceramics have high hardness and lubricity, allowing them to be
polished to a very smooth finish and to resist wear if used as bearing surfaces. Ceramics
also have good wettability, suggesting that lubricating layers can be used between ceramic
surfaces to reduce adhesive wear (eg, fretting) of these surfaces.
As bone graft substitutes because certain ceramics are osteoconductive and possibly
osteoinductive, supporting the attachment of osteogenic precursor cells.

Ceramics
Ceramics are solid, inorganic compounds consisting of metallic and nonmetallic
elements, such as oxygen (oxides), nitrogen (nitrides), carbon (carbides), chlorine
(chlorides), and silicon (silicides), bound by ionic or covalent bonds. They include
compounds such as silica (SiO2), alumina (Al2O3), silicon nitride (Si3N4), and titanium
carbide (TiC). Structural ceramics used in orthopaedic applications typically are three-
dimensional crystalline arrays of positively charged metal ions and negatively charged
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:26 PM
AAOS | Orthopaedic Biomaterials
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002108
19/44

nonmetal ions. If processed to high purity, ceramics have excellent biocompatibility
because of their insolubility and chemical inertness.
Ceramic Compounds
Alumina, in the form of aluminum oxide, is associated with lower rates of wear if used for
prosthetic bearings than conventional metal-on-polyethylene bearings. Although early clinical
experience found that the fracture of femoral heads made of alumina was a substantial
problem, this problem appears to be design-related rather than material-related. Newer
device designs have shown substantially lower fracture rates.
Zirconia, in the form of zirconium oxide (ZrO2), has shown less clinical success than alumina if
used as a bearing surface in contact with polyethylene. Zirconia has less toughness (lower
energy absorbance to surface failure, called fretting) than alumina, which makes it more
susceptible to roughening and increased wear.
Hydroxyapatite—Ca5(PO4)3(OH)—is a hydrated calcium phosphate that is similar in crystalline
structure to the hydroxyapatite that is the major mineral component of bone. Because of its
low solubility, hydroxyapatite is very slowly resorbed by the body.
β-tricalcium phosphate, α-tricalcium phosphate, and calcium sulfate are alternatives to
hydroxyapatite as bone-graft materials. These alternative materials have less strength and
faster resorption than hydroxyapatite but appear to have greater bioactivity because of their
increased solubility in aqueous environments.
Ceramic silica (SiO2) induces bone formation if combined with other ceramics, such as calcium
phosphate. Polymers are materials made of atoms of carbon and other elements that are
covalently bound to one another to form identical subunits, known as monomers (eg,
CH2=CH2). If the subunits bound to one another, often in repeating sequences, they form
chains (polymers) or sheets. Polymers (eg,—CH2—CH2—CH2—) typically are corrosion-
resistant, and many are flexible. Examples are polyethylene, polypropylene,
polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE, Teflon), silicones, and hydrogels.
Modern Ceramics
Ceramic materials have undergone multiple engineering innovations since their introduction in
arthroplasty in the early 1970s. Current ceramics used in joint replacement are fifth-
generation materials, which also are referred to as zirconia-toughened alumina matrix
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:26 PM
AAOS | Orthopaedic Biomaterials
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002108
20/44

composites. Zirconia-toughened alumina is comprised of alumina (82%), zirconia (17%),
strontium aluminate (0.5%), and chromium oxide (0.5%). Zirconia-toughened alumina, which
was clinically introduced in 2003, has demonstrated increased strength, fracture toughness,
and wear resistance compared with earlier ceramic materials.
Polymers
Polymers are large molecules consisting of combinations of smaller molecules. The properties
of a polymer are dictated by the following:
Its chemical structure (the monomer of which multiple units are linked together to create the
polymer)
Its molecular weight, which is determined by the number of monomers in the polymer
Its physical structure (the way in which the monomers are attached to each other within the
polymer)
Isomerism (the different orientations of atoms in some polymers)
Crystallinity (the packing of polymer chains into ordered atomic arrays).
Polymethyl methacrylate
Polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA, also known as Lucite or Plexiglas), is a bone cement and the
most commonly used polymer in orthopaedics.

Polymethyl methacrylate
PMMA is produced through an addition reaction in which molecules of methyl
methacrylate (liquid component) and the methyl ester of methacrylic acid (powder
component), become chemically bound to one another to generate PMMA, C5O2H8n.
Mixing of the liquid and powder components for the generation of PMMA results in an
exothermic reaction (with a temperature of approximately 82°C). Antibiotic agents can
be added to PMMA bone cement to provide prophylaxis or aid in the management of
infection. However, the addition of antibiotic agents during the mixing process used in
producing PMMA may adversely affect the properties of PMMA bone cement by
interfering with the crystallinity of the polymer. If antibiotic agents are added, they
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:26 PM
AAOS | Orthopaedic Biomaterials
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002108
21/44

should be combined in powder form with the powder component of the polymer and
thoroughly mixed before adding the liquid monomer. The performance of PMMA bone
cement has been enhanced through improved protocols in its handling, in bone
preparation, and in delivery of the cement to the site at which it acts. Vacuum-mixing or
centrifugation may decrease the porosity of PMMA cement, increasing its ultimate
tensile strength by approximately 40%.
Ultra-high-molecular-weight polyethylene
Ultra-high–molecular-weight polyethylene (UHMWPE) is another polymer commonly used in
orthopaedics.

Ultra-high-molecular-weight polyethylene
This long polyethylene polymer, —C2H4)n—, has a very high molecular weight, providing
substantially greater impact strength, greater toughness, and better abrasive wear
characteristics to the devices in which it is used than polyethylene of lower molecular
weights. UHMWPE used for orthopaedic devices is most commonly sterilized via gamma
irradiation. Four methods are used to fabricate orthopaedic components from UHMWPE:
(1) In ram extrusion, the semisolid resin of UHMWPE is extruded through a die under
heat and pressure to form a cylindrical bar that is then machined into a final shape. (2) In
compression molding, the resin of UHMWPE is modeled into a large sheet that is cut into
smaller pieces to use in machining of the final components of a prosthesis or other
device. (3) In direct molding, the resin of UHMWPE is directly molded into a finished part.
(4) Hot isostatic pressing (HIP’ing) involves a multistep conversion process that begins
with the manufacture of UHMWPE rods through cold isostatic pressing. The rods are
then sintered in a hot isostatic pressure. This conversion method is proprietary and used
by one orthopaedic manufacturer.

First-Generation Highly Cross-Linked Polyethylene
First-generation highly cross-linked polyethylene (HXLPE) was introduced in the late
1990s to help decrease wear. First-generation HXLPE is processed with a radiation dose
between 50 kGy and 105 kGy via a gamma or an e-beam irradiation source. After
irradiation, these materials undergo thermal processing below (annealing) or above

eliminate free radicals, which increases the risk of in vivo oxidation over time. Remelting
results in complete eradication of free radicals but decreases crystallinity, which may
increase the risk of plastic deformation and damage caused by impingement (eg, rim
fracture). The clinical performance of annealed and remelted first-generation HXLPE has
been successful.
Second-Generation HXLPE

Second-Generation HXLPE
Second-generation HXLPE was introduced in the mid-2000s to overcome the limitations
of first-generation HXLPE, including in vivo oxidation and rim fracture. These materials
are produced via three manufacture processes: the addition of antioxidants (eg, vitamin
E, phenols), mechanical annealing, and sequential irradiation and annealing. Clinical data
on second-generation HXLPE demonstrate excellent performance.

Bone
Bone is anisotropic because of the orientation of its components. The stiffness and
strength of bone and its storage of energy increase with the rate at which it is loaded (ie,
it is viscoelastic). Several radiographic studies have suggested that aging is associated
with bone remodeling that affects the force distribution within bone (the Wolff law).
Subperiosteal apposition of bone occurs in combination with endosteal absorption in
tubular bones, transforming these bones into cylinders of larger diameter. This is an
example of changing polar moment of inertia to maintain structural strength. This
remodeling of the diaphysis of long bones is hypothesized to serve a mechanical
compensatory function for environmental changes to the individual (eg, individual aging,
increased limb loading because of athletic activity, reduced loading because of space
flight). Stated simply, the bone is reshaped in terms of cross-sectional geometry and wall
thickness to best match the load environment imposed upon it. In older individuals, the
cross-sectional moment of inertia of long bones is remodeled so that if the cortical wall
thins, the load-bearing capacity is not lost. Essentially, the reshaping of the bone
compensates for the lost load-bearing capacity of a thin cortical wall so that load-bearing
capacity is retained.

perpendicular to that direction.

Biomaterials are used in orthopaedic surgery for the internal fixation of fractures,
osteotomies, and arthrodesis; in wound closure; as tissue substitutes; and in internal
prostheses (joint replacement). Orthopaedic biomaterials should be biocompatible by
minimizing detrimental local or systemic responses; resisting mechanical, chemical, and

application.

solely a function of geometry, independent of material properties, and is inversely
proportional to the stress caused by bending
Biocompatible material: A material that can function in a biologic environment without
known and/or substantial detrimental effects on the material or the living system
Biodegradable material: A material that breaks down when placed in a biologic environment

Coupling: Motion in which rotation or translation of a rigid body about one axis is associated

Creep: The increased deformation of a material over time in response to the application of a

Cross-linking: Association of adjacent polymers through covalent bonds
Ductile: A material that exhibits a considerable amount of plastic deformation before fracture

Extrusion: The process of heating and then forcing a material through a die to obtain a
continuous shape matching the cross-section of the die (eg, a duct or tube)
Elastic deformation: Deformation that disappears if the stress is removed
Elastic limit: Strain beyond which permanent deformation occurs
Elastic modulus: The numeric description of the deformation of an object under increasing

Endurance limit: The strength of a ferrous alloy after 106 loading cycles

Incompatible material: Elicits a destructive immunologic or inflammatory response (eg,
organ rejection)
Inert material: Elicits little or no host response
Interactive material: A material designed to elicit specific response from the host into which
it is implanted (eg, boney ingrowth into porous metals)
Isotropic material: A material that has the same mechanical properties along all of its internal
axes if subjected to loads
Load: The mechanical force that acts on an object
Material property: Any physical characteristic of an object’s substance (eg, heat conduction,
diffusivity, thermal expansion, and melting point) that is independent of the object’s structure
and geometry
Mechanical property: A subset of material properties that relates stresses to strains; for
linear elastic materials, the proportionality constants are the Young modulus, shear modulus,
Poisson ratio, etc.
Metal: A typically hard, durable, and malleable material consisting of metal atomic bonding
(eg, a sea of electrons). A metal consists of a single element (eg, iron, titanium, copper, or
silver), but a metal alloy is a solution of metallic and/or nonmetallic elements (eg, Ti-6Al-4V).
Modulus of elasticity: (Young modulus) A unique property of a material defined by the slope
of the linear portion of the stress-strain curve
Molecular weight: Mass, in grams, of 6.02 × 1023 (Avogadro number) molecules; for polymers,
the average molecular size; Mn is the number-average molecular weight and M2 is the weight-
average molecular weight.
Moment (also called torque): The tendency of a force, measured in Nm or ft-lb, to cause
rotations about an axis; a vector having a magnitude defined by the product of the magnitude
of the force and the perpendicular distance between the axis and the line of application of the
force.
Polymer: A material made of atoms of carbon and other elements that are covalently bound
to one another to form identical subunits, known as monomers (CH2=CH2), with the subunits
themselves also bound to one another, often in repeating sequences, to form chains or sheets
(—CH2—CH2—CH2—). PMMA (polymethyl methacrylate, C5O2H8n) is the most used polymer in
orthopaedics.
Poisson ratio: A material property defining the lateral expansion (or contraction) of a
deformable object transverse (at 90°) to the direction of loading; if an object is stretched, it
also will contract in the transverse direction, and vice versa.

Polar moment of inertia: A quantity determined by the cross-sectional area and distribution
of an object around a neutral axis upon torsional loading of the object
Resilience: The capacity of strained material to recover its size and shape after the deforming
load is removed
Strain: The deformation of a material by a force acting on a material or the change in the
length of a material under stress compared to the original length of the material relieved of
stress
Strength: Force applied over a unit of area
Stress: The force applied over a unit of area of a material
Stress relaxation: A decrease in the stress on a material over time as the result of a constant
displacement within the material or object
Toughness: The area under the stress-strain curve; it describes the energy needed to cause
the material to fail.
Ultimate strain: Maximum strain sustained by the specimen before failure of the material.
Viable material: Implanted biomaterial that incorporates and attracts cells and is then
absorbed and/or remodeled by the host (eg, biodegradable ceramic or polymeric scaffolds for
functional tissue engineering
Yield point: The transition between elastic and plastic deformation
